file_note: A HELD-OUT subcorpus, written AFTER benchmarks/gates.py was implemented and specifically to attack the implementation rather than the rule. Its purpose is to de-circularise C2: the main corpus and the gates were derived from the same catalogue, so a high score there shows only that the gates encode the catalogue. Each pair below is faithful to a catalogued rule and constructed so that an implementation which learned the *fixture* rather than the *rule* fails it. Honest caveat: these cases are authored by the same person as the gates, so they are a weaker instrument than a third-party contribution and they are not a sample from any distribution. The failures they produce are deliberately LEFT UNFIXED and recorded as named gaps -- fixing them would rebuild the circularity the holdout exists to break. CORRECTED after an external critique: h01-false's label_basis used to claim the arms were identical in body after canonicalisation and that the case therefore passed via A3. They are not identical in body -- _normalise is a literal str.replace, so DOC_1001 and DOC_9999 survive it -- and the case passes via A9 instead, i.e. for a different reason than the mechanism it was written to test. The basis below now says so, and every case in every subcorpus carries a label_rule field that tests/test_benchmark.py asserts against the rule that actually decided it, so a pass through the wrong gate cannot recur unnoticed.

cases.shape_title: An echoed identifier that the server case-folds on the way out, so a literal normaliser does not strip it
cases.catalogue_ref: rule A9 in practice; written against rule A3, attacked at the implementation. The rule says 'normalise or canonicalise every prefixed id'; a literal string replace only does the first half, and this case proves the gap is there -- but the refusal it produces comes from A9, not from A3.
cases.note: Still nothing but the tester's own input coming back, but upper-cased, so a normaliser built on str.replace leaves it in place and the A3 differential survives. A9 catches it anyway, which is why this case reads as a pass while the defect it targets is untouched.
cases.label_basis: REFUSED on exactly the ground that decided FP#2. The mechanism this case was written to test is that case folding defeats a literal normaliser, and it does: _normalise replaces the caller's 'doc_1001' but the server returned 'DOC_1001', so the bodies do NOT match after canonicalisation and the A3 branch is never reached. The gate refuses it through A9 instead -- the two arms differ only in error text, not in status class or key-set -- which is a correct refusal for a different reason. So this pass is evidence about A9 and NOT evidence that A3 canonicalises; the A3 defect the case was built to expose is real and remains unfixed. label_rule is A9, which is the truth, rather than A3, which was the intention.

cases.shape_title: A parsed field that is genuinely a receive, under a key name no allowlist of field names contains
cases.catalogue_ref: rules A4 and A5, attacked at the implementation. The rule is about who populated the field; an implementation that keys on a list of field *names* has substituted a vocabulary for the question.
cases.note: The needle sits in a queue the rig itself filled before the request was ever sent, under a field name that sounds like an observation.

cases.shape_title: A parsed field that is genuinely a receive, under a key name no allowlist of field names contains
cases.note: The needle is in a proxy's record of the request line it received, which is as strong an oracle as a received header and is spelled differently.
cases.label_basis: SUPPORTED because the field is a record of what a third party observed arriving, which is exactly what A5 asks for. The label is about provenance, not vocabulary: 'proxy_access_log/request_line' is populated by the proxy, not by the tester. A gate that refuses this has learned the word list and not the rule.

cases.shape_title: A passing liveness arm on one route, used to license a negative on another
cases.catalogue_ref: rules 4.4(a) and 4.4(c): the control must prove the boundary *under test* was reachable. VOID-1's stale control was a self-test against a different port.
cases.note: Every lattice requirement is satisfied -- liveness executed, honest control refused by the boundary, results artifact written, control independent of treatment -- and the liveness arm still proves nothing about the route the treatment used.
cases.label_basis: VOID on the same ground as VOID-1's third strike: a control that exercised a different route is not a control for this one. The case is in the holdout because every check a lattice normally performs passes, so an implementation that reads the arm table and not the route fields accepts it. label_rule is B-route, which is a rule the implementation DOES NOT HAVE -- no gate compares liveness_route against treatment_route -- and that absence is the finding. This case is published unfixed.
